title: What Would Change Your District's Mind About AI?
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky continues his year-long inquiry into AI in education by asking how districts can hold convictions firmly yet stay open to revision. He starts from the Latin root of conviction, which meant a legal verdict, and uses the wicked-problems framework to explain why districts must decide before evidence arrives. Drawing on research into compensatory conviction, moral conviction and identity-protective cognition, he shows how the phone-policy and AI-tutor studies get absorbed into prior commitments. He then surveys procedures from other fields, including clinical equipoise, adversarial collaboration, deliberative polling and incompletely theorized agreements. For schools he proposes concrete habits: write down in advance what evidence would change policy, pair an AI advocate with a skeptic on a project, and review past decisions on a schedule.
points: Potkalitsky argues that uncertainty tends to harden into certainty, so AI debates in education recycle the same positions.
The same studies on phone bans and AI tutoring get cited by opposing camps, which shows evidence being filtered by identity.
Medicine, behavioral science and deliberative democracy offer tested procedures for working with conviction rather than eliminating it.
A district AI committee can name in advance what evidence would change its policy, before the next landmark study appears.
The practical goal is a small shared agreement on next steps even when first principles still differ.
quotes: A conviction closes a case. A conviction grounds our values and orientation to the world.
Such problems have no definitive formulation and no stopping rule. Their solutions are better or worse, never true or false.
Add a research base that is still forming and you get a field where districts must decide before the evidence can tell them what to decide.
One camp reads the study as proof that AI damages learning. Another reads it as proof that design decides the outcome.
Students using unrestricted GPT-4 did better on practice and worse on later exams; a version built with tutoring guardrails largely avoided the harm.

A district AI committee might consider writing down what kinds of evidence would change its current policy before the next landmark, ground-breaking, norm-shattering study with a nifty title including some neologism is published.
In a pluralistic district (namely all of them) that may be the only kind of agreement available.
